# komposeauth integration guide (for LLMs and developers)

> How to sign users in to a frontend application with a komposeauth server, and how to protect a backend
> (resource server) with the tokens it issues. Every statement here is taken from the server's source code;
> file references are given so you can check them. Served by every running komposeauth instance at
> `/llms-full.txt` (index at `/llms.txt`).

Throughout this guide `https://auth.example.com` stands for the public base URL of the komposeauth server and
`https://api.example.com` for your own backend. Replace both.

---

## 1. What komposeauth is

- A **Spring Authorization Server** (OAuth 2.1 + OpenID Connect 1.0) backed by MongoDB, packaged as the Docker
  image `pitampoudel/komposeauth`.
- It signs **RS256 JWT access tokens**. Resource servers validate them locally with the public keys at
  `/oauth2/jwks`; they do not need to call the auth server per request.
- Sign-in methods: email or phone + password, Google, Apple (ID token), passkeys (WebAuthn), and one-time codes
  sent by SMS/WhatsApp or email. Users are created automatically on first Google, Apple or OTP sign-in.
- It also stores user profiles, roles, KYC records and organizations, exposed through a JSON API.
- A **Kotlin Multiplatform client SDK** (`io.github.pitampoudel:komposeauth-client`) wraps the API for
  Android, iOS, desktop and web Compose apps.

There are two independent ways for a frontend to get a token. Pick one per app:

| Approach | Use it for | Endpoint |
|---|---|---|
| **A. OAuth 2.1 authorization code + PKCE** (standard OIDC) | Any web SPA, server-rendered web app, native mobile app or third-party app. Works with any certified OIDC client library. The user signs in on the auth server's hosted login page. | `/oauth2/authorize`, `/oauth2/token` |
| **B. First-party JSON login API** | Your own apps that render their own login UI (the KMP SDK uses this). | `POST /login` |

Both produce JWTs signed by the same key, so a resource server validates them the same way (section 5).

---

## 2. Server facts you need before writing code

### 2.1 Discovery and protocol endpoints

| Purpose | Path | Auth |
|---|---|---|
| OIDC discovery document | `GET /.well-known/openid-configuration` | public |
| OAuth metadata | `GET /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` | public |
| Authorization endpoint | `GET /oauth2/authorize` | browser session (redirects to `/session-login`) |
| Token endpoint | `POST /oauth2/token` (form-encoded) | `client_id` |
| JSON Web Key Set | `GET /oauth2/jwks` | public |
| OIDC UserInfo | `GET /userinfo` | Bearer access token with `openid` scope |
| Token revocation | `POST /oauth2/revoke` | client |
| Token introspection | `POST /oauth2/introspect` | client |
| Hosted login page | `GET /session-login` | public |

Always read the actual URLs from the discovery document instead of hard-coding them when your library supports
discovery.

### 2.2 The issuer (`iss`)

The server has no fixed issuer setting. The issuer is derived from each request's scheme, host and port
(`core/utils/ServerUtils.kt`, Spring Authorization Server defaults), so it equals the public URL the client used,
e.g. `https://auth.example.com` with no trailing slash. Consequences:

- Behind a proxy the server must see the original scheme and host (`FORWARD_HEADERS_STRATEGY=framework`, the
  default, and a proxy that sends `X-Forwarded-Proto`/`X-Forwarded-Host`). Otherwise `iss` becomes
  `http://internal-host:8080` and validation fails.
- Always reach the auth server by one canonical public URL, from browsers and from backends alike.

### 2.3 Registering an OAuth client (needed for approach A)

An administrator registers clients, either on the admin console at `https://auth.example.com/admin/clients`, or
through the API with an ADMIN token:

```http
POST /oauth2/clients
Authorization: Bearer <admin access token>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "clientName": "My Web App",
  "redirectUris": ["https://app.example.com/callback", "http://localhost:5173/callback"],
  "accessTokenTtlSeconds": 900,
  "refreshTokenTtlDays": 30,
  "scopes": ["openid", "profile", "email"]
}
```

Response (the secret is generated when you omit `clientSecret`):

```json
{
  "clientName": "My Web App",
  "clientId": "66f1c0e4a1b2c3d4e5f60718",
  "clientSecret": "...64 hex chars...",
  "redirectUris": ["https://app.example.com/callback", "http://localhost:5173/callback"],
  "clientUri": null,
  "logoUri": null,
  "scopes": ["openid", "profile", "email"],
  "accessTokenTtlSeconds": 900,
  "refreshTokenTtlDays": 30
}
```

What every registered client gets (`oauth_clients/dto/Mappers.kt`):

- Grant types: `authorization_code`, `refresh_token`, `client_credentials`.
- Client authentication methods: `none` (public) and `client_secret_post`.
- **PKCE is required** (`requireProofKey = true`). Every authorization request must carry `code_challenge` and
  `code_challenge_method=S256`, including from server-side apps.
- No consent screen (`requireAuthorizationConsent = false`).
- `redirect_uri` must match a registered URI exactly.
- `accessTokenTtlSeconds` is at least 60; `refreshTokenTtlDays` at least 1.
- `clientId` is a 24-character MongoDB ObjectId hex string. If you supply one it must be in that format.
- If `scopes` is omitted it defaults to `openid profile email offline_access user.read.any`. `user.read.any`
  lets the client read **every** user's record (section 6). Only grant it to trusted backend clients; pass an
  explicit `scopes` list for browser and mobile apps.

### 2.3a Clients identified by a metadata document (no registration)

A client may instead use an HTTPS URL as its `client_id`, serving its metadata there as JSON (a Client ID
Metadata Document, draft-ietf-oauth-client-id-metadata-document, used by the MCP authorization spec and by
clients such as Claude). The server fetches the document when the client first appears and caches it for 10
minutes (`oauth_clients/cimd/ClientIdMetadataDocuments.kt`); discovery advertises
`client_id_metadata_document_supported: true`. Such a client:

- must serve a document whose `client_id` equals its URL, with `redirect_uris` (HTTPS, or `http` on a loopback
  address) and `token_endpoint_auth_method` `none` (or absent); hosts on private networks aren't fetched;
- is a public client: authorization code with PKCE, plus `refresh_token` if its `grant_types` list it;
- gets only `openid profile email`, and always shows the user a **consent screen** naming its URL;
- gets 1-hour access tokens and 30-day refresh tokens that are **rotated** on every use.

### 2.4 CORS and cookies

- Browser apps calling the auth server from another origin (token endpoint, `/login`, `/me`, ...) must have their
  origin listed under **CORS allowed origins** on the configuration page `https://auth.example.com/admin/config`.
  Wildcard patterns such as `https://*.example.com` are accepted. Credentials are allowed.
- The access-token cookie is named `access_token`, is `HttpOnly`, `Secure` + `SameSite=None` over HTTPS, and is
  scoped to the **relying party ID** (`rpId` on the configuration page, e.g. `example.com`), so it is shared with
  every subdomain of that domain. Without an `rpId` it is host-only.
- The server's security filter chains currently have CSRF protection disabled
  (`core/security/WebSecurityConfig.kt`), so no CSRF token is needed for cookie-authenticated writes.

---

## 3. Frontend integration

### 3.1 Approach A: authorization code + PKCE (recommended for web and third-party apps)

Flow:

1. Generate `code_verifier` (43-128 random URL-safe characters) and `code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier))`.
2. Redirect the browser to:
   ```
   https://auth.example.com/oauth2/authorize
     ?response_type=code
     &client_id=<clientId>
     &redirect_uri=<registered redirect uri, URL-encoded>
     &scope=openid%20profile%20email
     &state=<random>
     &nonce=<random>
     &code_challenge=<challenge>
     &code_challenge_method=S256
   ```
   Optional parameters:
   - `prompt=login` or `prompt=select_account`: force the login page even if the user already has a session
     on the auth server (use for "switch account"). `prompt=none`: fail with `login_required` instead of showing a
     page.
   - `idp=google`: skip the login page and send the user straight to Google (only if Google is configured).
3. The user signs in on `/session-login` (password, Google, and whatever else the operator enabled). The server
   redirects to `redirect_uri?code=...&state=...`. Check `state`.
4. Exchange the code (form-encoded POST):
   ```http
   POST /oauth2/token
   Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

   grant_type=authorization_code&code=<code>&redirect_uri=<same uri>&client_id=<clientId>&code_verifier=<verifier>
   ```
   Response:
   ```json
   {
     "access_token": "eyJ...",
     "token_type": "Bearer",
     "expires_in": 899,
     "scope": "openid profile email",
     "id_token": "eyJ..."
   }
   ```
5. Send `Authorization: Bearer <access_token>` to your resource servers.

Client authentication at the token endpoint: whenever the form contains `client_id`, the server authenticates the
request as a **public client** (`core/providers/OAuth2PublicClientAuthConverter.kt`), so a browser app never needs
the client secret. Never ship the client secret in browser or mobile code.

Refresh tokens: the authorization-code exchange returns a `refresh_token`, public clients included (komposeauth
issues one to every client with the `refresh_token` grant, which all registered clients have; stock Spring
Authorization Server would withhold it from public clients). It lasts the client's `refreshTokenTtlDays` and is
reused, not rotated: refreshing returns a new access token and the same refresh token. Refresh with a form POST
to the token endpoint, again with `client_id` and no secret:

```http
POST /oauth2/token
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=refresh_token&refresh_token=<refresh_token>&client_id=<clientId>
```

If the refresh is rejected (expired or revoked), run the authorize redirect again: while the user still has a
session on the auth server (24 hours by default, `SESSION_TIMEOUT`) it completes without a login page.
`prompt=none` makes that explicit. Iframe-based silent renew does not work because the server forbids framing.

Logout: clear your own tokens, then end the auth server session with the `end_session_endpoint` from the discovery
document (RP-initiated logout, pass `id_token_hint` and a `post_logout_redirect_uri`) or with `GET /logout` on the
auth server using the browser's session.

#### Example: SPA with `oidc-client-ts`

```ts
import { UserManager, WebStorageStateStore } from "oidc-client-ts";

export const auth = new UserManager({
  authority: "https://auth.example.com",          // discovery is read from /.well-known/openid-configuration
  client_id: "66f1c0e4a1b2c3d4e5f60718",
  redirect_uri: `${window.location.origin}/callback`,
  post_logout_redirect_uri: window.location.origin,
  response_type: "code",                           // PKCE S256 is automatic
  scope: "openid profile email",
  automaticSilentRenew: true,                      // renews with the refresh token, no iframe involved
  userStore: new WebStorageStateStore({ store: window.sessionStorage }),
});

// Login button
await auth.signinRedirect();

// /callback route
const user = await auth.signinRedirectCallback();

// Calling your API
const current = await auth.getUser();
if (!current || current.expired) {
  await auth.signinRedirect();                     // refresh token gone: completes silently while the auth-server session lives
} else {
  await fetch("https://api.example.com/orders", {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${current.access_token}` },
  });
}
```

The SPA's origin must be in the CORS allow-list, because `oidc-client-ts` fetches the discovery document, the JWKS
and the token endpoint from the browser.

#### Example: server-rendered app (Next.js / Express / Django / Rails)

Use your framework's OIDC client (Auth.js, `openid-client`, `authlib`, `omniauth_openid_connect`, ...) with:

- issuer / authority: `https://auth.example.com`
- client id: the registered `clientId`
- PKCE enabled with S256 (required even for server-side apps)
- token endpoint auth method: `none` (or `client_secret_post`; the server treats both as public)
- scopes: `openid profile email`
- keep the access token in the server-side session and forward it as `Authorization: Bearer` when calling APIs.

Auth.js (NextAuth) provider:

```ts
{
  id: "komposeauth",
  name: "komposeauth",
  type: "oidc",
  issuer: "https://auth.example.com",
  clientId: process.env.KOMPOSEAUTH_CLIENT_ID,
  client: { token_endpoint_auth_method: "none" },
  checks: ["pkce", "state", "nonce"],
  authorization: { params: { scope: "openid profile email" } },
}
```

#### Example: native mobile apps (AppAuth for Android/iOS, `expo-auth-session`, `flutter_appauth`)

Register a redirect URI with a private scheme, e.g. `com.example.app:/oauth2redirect`, and configure the library
with the discovery URL, the `clientId`, that redirect URI, scopes `openid profile email` and PKCE (on by default in
these libraries). Private-scheme redirects are supported. Kotlin Multiplatform apps should use the SDK instead
(section 3.3).

### 3.2 Approach B: the first-party JSON login API

`POST /login?responseType=<TOKEN|COOKIE|SESSION>` with a JSON body. The body is a tagged union discriminated by
`"type"` (`shared/.../user/data/Credential.kt`):

| `type` | Fields | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `USERNAME_PASSWORD` | `username`, `password`, optional `countryNameCode` | `username` is an email or phone number; `countryNameCode` (e.g. `"NP"`) lets a local phone number be parsed. |
| `OTP` | `username`, `otp` | Code previously sent with `POST /send-otp`. Creates the user if new. |
| `GOOGLE_ID` | `idToken` | A Google ID token for the Google client ID the server is configured with. |
| `APPLE_ID` | `idToken` | A Sign in with Apple ID token. |
| `AUTH_CODE` | `platform` (`WEB`, `DESKTOP`, `ANDROID`, `IOS`), `code`, `redirectUri` | A Google OAuth authorization code; the server exchanges it. |
| `PUBLIC_KEY` | `authenticationResponseJson` | WebAuthn assertion (see below). |
| `REFRESH_TOKEN` | `refreshToken` | A refresh token returned earlier by this endpoint. |

`responseType`:

- `TOKEN`: body is `{"access_token","token_type":"Bearer","expires_in":86400,"refresh_token"}`. Use this for
  mobile, desktop and any app that stores tokens itself.
- `COOKIE` (the default): sets the HttpOnly `access_token` cookie and returns the user profile. Use this for a
  browser app on a subdomain of the relying-party ID; call with `credentials: "include"`.
- `SESSION`: creates a server session on the auth server and returns the profile.

Tokens from `/login` last 24 hours. The refresh token lasts 30 days and is **single-use**: each refresh returns a
new access token and a new refresh token; store the new one and discard the old. Presenting a spent refresh token
returns 400.

```bash
# Password login, tokens in the body
curl -X POST 'https://auth.example.com/login?responseType=TOKEN' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"type":"USERNAME_PASSWORD","username":"ada@example.com","password":"correct horse"}'

# Refresh
curl -X POST 'https://auth.example.com/login?responseType=TOKEN' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"type":"REFRESH_TOKEN","refreshToken":"<refresh_token>"}'
```

```ts
// Browser app on app.example.com with rpId = example.com: cookie login
await fetch("https://auth.example.com/login?responseType=COOKIE", {
  method: "POST",
  credentials: "include",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  body: JSON.stringify({ type: "USERNAME_PASSWORD", username, password }),
});
// Later requests to *.example.com send the cookie; resource servers can read it (section 5.7).
```

One-time code sign-in:

```bash
curl -X POST https://auth.example.com/send-otp -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"username":"+9779812345678","type":"PHONE"}'        # or "type":"EMAIL" with an email address
curl -X POST 'https://auth.example.com/login?responseType=TOKEN' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"type":"OTP","username":"+9779812345678","otp":"123456"}'
```

Passkey sign-in: `GET /login-options?platform=WEB` returns `{"googleClientId", "publicKeyAuthOptionsJson"}` and
stores the WebAuthn challenge in a session cookie. Pass `publicKeyAuthOptionsJson` to
`navigator.credentials.get()`, then post the serialized result as
`{"type":"PUBLIC_KEY","authenticationResponseJson":"..."}` to `/login` **with the same cookie**
(`credentials: "include"`). Registering a passkey for a signed-in user: `POST /webauthn/register/options`, then
`POST /webauthn/register` with `{"publicKey": ...}`.

Logout: `GET` or `POST /logout` clears the cookie and the server session. Bearer-token apps simply delete their
stored tokens.

Error responses are RFC 7807 problem details (`{"type","title","status","detail"}`): 400 for malformed input or a
bad/spent token or OTP, 401 for a missing, expired or invalid bearer token, 403 for wrong credentials, a
deactivated account or insufficient rights, 409 for a duplicate email/phone, 429 when rate limited.

### 3.3 Kotlin Multiplatform / Compose Multiplatform apps: use the SDK

```kotlin
// build.gradle.kts
implementation("io.github.pitampoudel:komposeauth-client:<version>")   // includes komposeauth-shared
```

```kotlin
val httpClient = HttpClient {
    installKomposeAuth(
        // Android overload takes a Context first: installKomposeAuth(context, authServerUrl, resourceServerUrls)
        authServerUrl = "https://auth.example.com",
        resourceServerUrls = listOf("https://api.example.com")
    )
}
initializeKomposeAuth(httpClient = httpClient)   // registers Koin modules and ViewModels
```

What the SDK does (`client/.../core/data/installKomposeAuth.kt`): persists tokens, adds
`Authorization: Bearer` to requests whose host is the auth server or one of `resourceServerUrls`, refreshes on 401
with the `REFRESH_TOKEN` credential, and clears tokens when the refresh is rejected. Use `LoginViewModel` with
`rememberKmpCredentialManager()` for Google/passkey sign-in, `OtpViewModel` for codes, `ProfileViewModel`,
`KycViewModel`, and `rememberCurrentUser()` for the signed-in user. Your resource servers only have to validate the
bearer token.

### 3.4 Reading the current user in a frontend

- `GET /me` (Bearer or cookie) returns the profile:
  ```json
  {
    "id": "66f1...", "givenName": "Ada", "familyName": "Lovelace",
    "email": "ada@example.com", "phoneNumber": "+9779812345678",
    "emailVerified": true, "phoneNumberVerified": false, "kycVerified": false,
    "picture": "https://...", "createdAt": "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z", "updatedAt": "...",
    "socialLinks": [], "roles": ["ADMIN"]
  }
  ```
- `GET /userinfo` returns the OIDC UserInfo for an access token with the `openid` scope.
- Or decode the ID token / access token claims (section 4). Do not use unverified claims for authorization in
  the frontend; that is the resource server's job.
- Update the profile: `POST /update-profile` with any of `givenName`, `familyName`, `email`, `password` +
  `confirmPassword`, `currentPassword` (required to change the password or email of an account that has one),
  `picture`.
- Password reset: `PUT /reset-password?email=<email>` emails a link; the rest happens on the server's own pages.

---

## 4. Token reference

All tokens are JWS compact JWTs signed with **RS256**. The header carries a `kid` matching a key in
`/oauth2/jwks`.

### 4.1 Access token claims

| Claim | Present in | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `iss` | all | Auth server public URL (section 2.2) |
| `sub` | all | **User id** (24-char hex). For `client_credentials` tokens it is the client id. |
| `aud` | authorization-code tokens | The OAuth `client_id`. Tokens from `/login` have **no `aud`**. |
| `exp`, `iat`, `nbf` | all | Standard times (seconds) |
| `scope` | all | JSON array of scope strings, e.g. `["openid","profile","email"]` |
| `authorities` | user tokens | JSON array of roles, **prefixed**: `["ROLE_ADMIN"]` (empty for users with no role) |
| `email` | user tokens, if the user has one | |
| `givenName`, `familyName` | user tokens, if set | camelCase, **not** `given_name` / `family_name` |
| `picture` | user tokens, if set | URL |
| `kycVerified` | user tokens | boolean |
| `phoneNumberVerified` | user tokens | boolean |

Sources: `core/security/WebAuthorizationConfig.kt` (`jwtCustomizer`) and
`user/controller/ResourceOwnerLoginController.kt`. The ID token from the authorization-code flow carries the same
custom claims plus the standard OIDC ones (`nonce`, `auth_time`, ...).

### 4.2 UserInfo claims (`GET /userinfo`)

`sub`, `emailVerified`, `phoneNumberVerified`, `kycVerified`, `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `roles` (unprefixed, e.g.
`["ADMIN"]`), and when set `email`, `givenName`, `familyName`, `picture`.

### 4.3 Roles and scopes

- New users have no roles (`authorities` is `[]`). The built-in roles are `ADMIN` and `SUPER_ADMIN`
  (`SUPER_ADMIN` implies `ADMIN`); operators define their own in the roles catalog on the configuration page and
  grant them with `POST /users/{id}/roles/{role}`.
- Roles appear in tokens as `ROLE_<NAME>` inside `authorities`. Scopes appear in `scope`; the auth server itself
  maps them to Spring authorities `SCOPE_<scope>`.
- Special scopes: `user.read.any` (read any user via the API), `user.write.any` (create, deactivate, delete users).
- Role changes only show up in tokens issued after the change. With 24-hour `/login` tokens, a revoked role can
  stay in a live token until it expires; call `GET /users/{id}` if you need the current value.

### 4.4 Lifetimes

| Token | Lifetime |
|---|---|
| `/login` access token | 24 h |
| `/login` refresh token | 30 days, single use, rotated |
| Authorization-code refresh token | per client, `refreshTokenTtlDays`; reusable, not rotated |
| Authorization-code access token | per client, `accessTokenTtlSeconds` (default 900 s, min 60 s) |
| Auth-server browser session | `SESSION_TIMEOUT`, default 24 h |

---

## 5. Resource-server (backend API) integration

### 5.1 Rules

1. Read the token from `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>`. Optionally also from the `access_token` cookie if your API is
   on a subdomain of the relying-party ID and your browser app uses cookie login.
2. Verify the RS256 signature with keys from `https://auth.example.com/oauth2/jwks`. Cache the JWKS and refetch
   when a token has an unknown `kid` (standard JWKS libraries do this).
3. Check `exp` and `nbf` (allow ~60 s clock skew).
4. Check `iss == "https://auth.example.com"` (exact string, no trailing slash).
5. **Do not require `aud`** unless you only accept authorization-code tokens from specific clients: tokens from
   `/login` (and so from the KMP SDK) have no audience. If you do check it, allow the client ids you trust.
6. Authorize with `authorities` (roles, `ROLE_` prefixed) and `scope`. Identify the user by `sub`.
7. Reject with 401 and `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token"` on any failure; 403 when authenticated but
   not allowed.
8. The resource server does not need a client id or secret just to validate tokens.

If your API is called from browsers on other origins, configure CORS on the API itself; the auth server's CORS list
does not apply to your API.

### 5.2 Spring Boot (Spring Security resource server)

```kotlin
// build.gradle.kts
implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server")
```

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          issuer-uri: https://auth.example.com              # validates iss
          jwk-set-uri: https://auth.example.com/oauth2/jwks # keys (no discovery call needed at startup)
```

```kotlin
@Configuration
@EnableMethodSecurity
class SecurityConfig {
    @Bean
    fun jwtAuthenticationConverter() = JwtAuthenticationConverter().apply {
        // Roles already carry the ROLE_ prefix; scopes get SCOPE_. Mirrors the auth server's own converter.
        setJwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter { jwt ->
            (jwt.getClaimAsStringList("authorities").orEmpty().map { SimpleGrantedAuthority(it) } +
             jwt.getClaimAsStringList("scope").orEmpty().map { SimpleGrantedAuthority("SCOPE_$it") })
        }
    }

    @Bean
    fun filterChain(http: HttpSecurity, converter: JwtAuthenticationConverter): SecurityFilterChain = http
        .csrf { it.disable() }
        .sessionManagement { it.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS) }
        .authorizeHttpRequests {
            it.requestMatchers("/public/**").permitAll()
              .requestMatchers("/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
              .anyRequest().authenticated()
        }
        .oauth2ResourceServer { it.jwt { jwt -> jwt.jwtAuthenticationConverter(converter) } }
        .build()
}

@RestController
class OrdersController {
    @GetMapping("/orders")
    fun orders(@AuthenticationPrincipal jwt: Jwt): List<Order> = service.ordersFor(userId = jwt.subject)

    @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
    @DeleteMapping("/orders/{id}")
    fun delete(@PathVariable id: String) = service.delete(id)
}
```

To also accept the `access_token` cookie, register a `BearerTokenResolver` bean that falls back to the cookie when
the header is absent (the auth server does exactly this in `WebAuthorizationConfig.bearerTokenResolver`). Enable
CSRF protection on your API if you accept cookies.

### 5.3 Node.js (Express / Fastify / NestJS) with `jose`

```ts
import { createRemoteJWKSet, jwtVerify, type JWTPayload } from "jose";

const ISSUER = "https://auth.example.com";
const JWKS = createRemoteJWKSet(new URL(`${ISSUER}/oauth2/jwks`)); // cached, refetched on unknown kid

export interface KomposeClaims extends JWTPayload {
  authorities?: string[]; scope?: string[]; email?: string;
  givenName?: string; familyName?: string; picture?: string;
  kycVerified?: boolean; phoneNumberVerified?: boolean;
}

export async function verify(token: string): Promise<KomposeClaims> {
  const { payload } = await jwtVerify<KomposeClaims>(token, JWKS, {
    issuer: ISSUER,
    algorithms: ["RS256"],
    clockTolerance: 60,
  });
  return payload;
}

// Express middleware
export function requireAuth(role?: string) {
  return async (req, res, next) => {
    const header = req.headers.authorization ?? "";
    const token = header.startsWith("Bearer ") ? header.slice(7) : req.cookies?.access_token;
    if (!token) return res.status(401).set("WWW-Authenticate", "Bearer").end();
    try {
      const claims = await verify(token);
      if (role && !claims.authorities?.includes(`ROLE_${role}`)) return res.status(403).end();
      req.user = { id: claims.sub!, ...claims };
      next();
    } catch {
      res.status(401).set("WWW-Authenticate", 'Bearer error="invalid_token"').end();
    }
  };
}

app.get("/orders", requireAuth(), (req, res) => res.json(listOrders(req.user.id)));
app.delete("/orders/:id", requireAuth("ADMIN"), handler);
```

### 5.4 Python (FastAPI) with PyJWT

```python
import jwt                                   # pip install "pyjwt[crypto]"
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, HTTPException, Request

ISSUER = "https://auth.example.com"
jwks_client = jwt.PyJWKClient(f"{ISSUER}/oauth2/jwks", cache_keys=True)

def current_user(request: Request) -> dict:
    auth = request.headers.get("authorization", "")
    token = auth[7:] if auth.lower().startswith("bearer ") else request.cookies.get("access_token")
    if not token:
        raise HTTPException(401, headers={"WWW-Authenticate": "Bearer"})
    try:
        key = jwks_client.get_signing_key_from_jwt(token).key
        return jwt.decode(token, key, algorithms=["RS256"], issuer=ISSUER, leeway=60,
                          options={"verify_aud": False})   # /login tokens have no aud
    except jwt.PyJWTError:
        raise HTTPException(401, headers={"WWW-Authenticate": 'Bearer error="invalid_token"'})

def require_role(role: str):
    def check(user: dict = Depends(current_user)) -> dict:
        if f"ROLE_{role}" not in user.get("authorities", []):
            raise HTTPException(403)
        return user
    return check

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/orders")
def orders(user: dict = Depends(current_user)):
    return list_orders(user["sub"])

@app.delete("/orders/{order_id}")
def delete(order_id: str, user: dict = Depends(require_role("ADMIN"))):
    ...
```

### 5.5 Go with `golang-jwt` and `keyfunc`

```go
import (
    "github.com/MicahParks/keyfunc/v3"
    "github.com/golang-jwt/jwt/v5"
)

const issuer = "https://auth.example.com"

type Claims struct {
    Authorities []string `json:"authorities"`
    Scope       []string `json:"scope"`
    Email       string   `json:"email"`
    jwt.RegisteredClaims
}

jwks, _ := keyfunc.NewDefault([]string{issuer + "/oauth2/jwks"}) // refreshes in the background

func Verify(raw string) (*Claims, error) {
    claims := &Claims{}
    _, err := jwt.ParseWithClaims(raw, claims, jwks.Keyfunc,
        jwt.WithIssuer(issuer), jwt.WithValidMethods([]string{"RS256"}), jwt.WithLeeway(time.Minute))
    return claims, err // claims.Subject is the user id
}
```

### 5.6 Ktor server

```kotlin
install(Authentication) {
    jwt("komposeauth") {
        val issuer = "https://auth.example.com"
        val jwkProvider = JwkProviderBuilder(URI("$issuer/oauth2/jwks").toURL())
            .cached(10, 24, TimeUnit.HOURS).rateLimited(10, 1, TimeUnit.MINUTES).build()
        verifier(jwkProvider, issuer) { acceptLeeway(60) }
        validate { cred -> if (cred.payload.subject != null) JWTPrincipal(cred.payload) else null }
    }
}

routing {
    authenticate("komposeauth") {
        get("/orders") {
            val p = call.principal<JWTPrincipal>()!!
            val roles = p.payload.getClaim("authorities").asList(String::class.java).orEmpty()
            call.respond(listOrders(userId = p.payload.subject))
        }
    }
}
```

### 5.7 Accepting the cookie

Only relevant when a browser app uses `responseType=COOKIE` and your API is on a subdomain of the relying-party ID
(e.g. API `api.example.com`, auth `auth.example.com`, `rpId` `example.com`). The cookie `access_token` holds the
same JWT; validate it exactly like a bearer token. The browser must send it with `credentials: "include"`, and your
API's CORS must allow that origin with credentials. Protect state-changing endpoints against CSRF (e.g. require a
custom header or a CSRF token) because cookies are sent automatically.

---

## 6. Calling the auth server's API from a backend

A resource server sometimes needs data about other users (e.g. to show an author's name). Options:

1. **Forward the user's token**: call `GET https://auth.example.com/me` with the incoming bearer token.
2. **Service credentials**: register a dedicated OAuth client for the backend with scope `user.read.any`, keep its
   secret on the server only, and get a token with the client credentials grant:
   ```bash
   curl -X POST https://auth.example.com/oauth2/token \
     -d grant_type=client_credentials -d client_id=<id> -d client_secret=<secret> -d scope=user.read.any
   ```
   Then call:
   - `GET /users/{id}` - one user
   - `GET /users?ids=a,b,c` or `GET /users?q=<search>&role=<ROLE>&page=0&size=50` - paged
     `{"items":[...],"page","pageSize","totalItems","hasNext"}`
   - `GET /stats` - `{"totalUsers"}`
   With `user.write.any` it can also call `PATCH /users` (find or create a user from
   `{"email"|"phoneNumber", "firstName", "lastName", "password", "confirmPassword"}`),
   `POST /users/{id}/deactivate` and `DELETE /users/{id}`.
   Cache the client-credentials token until shortly before `expires_in`.

---

## 7. HTTP API summary

Paths are relative to the auth server. "User" means any authenticated user (Bearer or cookie). JSON bodies unless
stated. Admin-only endpoints accept `ADMIN` or `SUPER_ADMIN`.

| Method & path | Who | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /login?responseType=` | public | Sign in with a credential (section 3.2) |
| `GET/POST /logout` | public | Clear cookie and session |
| `GET /login-options?platform=` | public | Google client id + WebAuthn request options |
| `POST /send-otp` | public (optional auth) | `{"username","type":"PHONE"|"EMAIL"}` |
| `POST /verify-otp` | user | `{"username","type","otp"}` verify a phone/email on the current account |
| `GET /verify-email?token=` | public | Email verification link target |
| `PUT /reset-password?email=` | public | Send a reset link |
| `GET /me` | user | Current profile |
| `POST /update-profile` | user | Update profile (section 3.4) |
| `POST /webauthn/register/options`, `POST /webauthn/register` | user | Register a passkey |
| `GET /kyc`, `POST /kyc/personal-info`, `POST /kyc/address`, `POST /kyc/documents` | user | KYC submission |
| `GET /third-factor-kyc` | user | URL for third-party KYC verification |
| `GET /organizations?ids=`, `GET /organizations/{id}`, `POST /organizations`, `DELETE /organizations/{id}` | user | Organizations: list yours (or by `ids`), read, create or update, delete |
| `GET /users/{id}` | self, admin, or `user.read.any` | One user |
| `GET /users`, `GET /stats` | admin or `user.read.any` | List / count users |
| `PATCH /users`, `POST /users/{id}/deactivate`, `DELETE /users/{id}` | admin or `user.write.any` | Manage users |
| `GET /roles`, `POST|DELETE /users/{id}/roles/{role}` | admin | Roles |
| `GET /kyc/pending`, `POST /kyc/{id}/approve`, `POST /kyc/{id}/reject` | admin | Review KYC |
| `GET|POST|DELETE /oauth2/clients` | admin | OAuth clients |
| `GET /countries.json` | public | Country list for phone pickers |
| `GET /actuator/health/readiness` | public | Health probe |

For exact request and response schemas, read the DTOs in `shared/src/commonMain/kotlin/pitampoudel/komposeauth/`
or open Swagger UI at `/swagger-ui.html` as an admin.

---

## 8. Common mistakes

- Omitting PKCE. Every authorization request needs `code_challenge` + `code_challenge_method=S256`.
- A `redirect_uri` that differs from the registered one by a trailing slash, port or scheme.
- Validating `aud` and then rejecting every token from `/login` or the KMP SDK (they have no `aud`).
- Looking for `given_name`/`family_name`/`roles` in the access token. Use `givenName`, `familyName` and
  `authorities` (with `ROLE_` prefix). `/userinfo` has unprefixed `roles`.
- Hard-coding an issuer with a trailing slash, or reaching the auth server through an internal hostname so `iss`
  does not match.
- Sending the user back through the authorize redirect on every access-token expiry instead of using the
  `refresh_token` from the authorization-code exchange (section 3.1).
- Reusing a `/login` refresh token after it has been redeemed; always store the new one.
- Forgetting to add the browser app's origin to the auth server's CORS list (token endpoint and `/login` calls
  fail as opaque CORS errors).
- Putting the client secret in browser or mobile code. Only backend clients using `client_credentials` need it.
- Registering a browser client without an explicit `scopes` list, which grants `user.read.any` by default.
- Sending `/login` as form data. It takes JSON with a `"type"` discriminator; `/oauth2/token` takes form data.
